tagline: Google Drive, but your files live in your own Telegram, GitHub or S3.
summary: BYOS is a drive cut in half. Postgres remembers everything about your files; the bytes go to storage you already own. One Telegram code makes your account and connects your storage. Bao, an agent on your own LLM key, answers with checked citations and drafts changes as plans you approve.

features.name: Sign up with Telegram
features.summary: One Telegram code makes your account and plugs in your storage.
features.description: Pick a username and password, enter your phone, then type the code Telegram sends inside the app (not by SMS). Got two-step verification on? There's one more password step. Errors say what actually went wrong, like a taken username.
features.underTheHood: No user exists until the code checks out, so the half-finished sign-up rides in the browser as a Fernet-encrypted ticket that dies in 10 minutes. The server keeps zero pending state. On success, the user and their Telegram storage are created in one commit.

steps.label: fills the form
steps.narration: You pick a username and password. The page checks the password rules before bothering the server.

steps.label: sends sign-up details
steps.narration: The server checks the username is free, then hashes the password straight into the ticket.

steps.label: asks for a code
steps.narration: Telegram sends the code to your Telegram app. No SMS involved.

steps.label: encrypted ticket
steps.narration: The browser holds the whole half-finished sign-up for 10 minutes. The server remembers nothing.

steps.label: sends the code
steps.narration: The code goes back with the ticket. If your Telegram has 2FA, it asks for that password too.

steps.label: user + storage
steps.narration: One transaction creates your account and hooks up Telegram as storage. All or nothing.

steps.label: tokens + cookie
steps.narration: You get a 15-minute access token kept in memory, plus a refresh cookie JavaScript can't touch.

keyFiles: apps/web/components/auth/auth-shell.tsx — steps indicator, code input, Bao panel

deep.algorithm: Stateless multi-step login via encrypted tickets
deep.idea: Every half-finished login step lives in an encrypted, expiring ticket the browser carries, so the server stores nothing until Telegram verifies the code.
how: start_signup checks the username, Argon2-hashes the password, and asks Telegram to send a code.
The ticket holds phone, phone_code_hash, the partial Telethon StringSession, awaiting='code' and signup fields, Fernet-encrypted.
verify_code decrypts it with a 600 s TTL, rejects it if awaiting doesn't match, and calls sign_in.
2FA accounts get a fresh ticket with awaiting='password'; verify_password finishes sign_in.
_complete creates the user and Telegram storage account in one commit, then issues JWT + refresh cookie.
deep.why: No user exists until the code verifies, so a pending-logins table would need cleanup and could leave half-made accounts. Fernet makes the ticket opaque, tamper-proof and self-expiring.
deep.cost: Two to three Telegram round-trips; zero server state between steps.

stepNotes.2: start_signup checks the username is free (a read, nothing written), Argon2-hashes the password and asks Telegram for a code. The ticket is then Fernet-encrypted with {phone, phone_code_hash, session, username, password_hash, awaiting:'code'}. Fernet stamps the time, so decrypt_ttl(ticket, 600) rejects it after 10 minutes.
stepNotes.3: A fresh Telethon client calls send_code_request(phone). The ticket gains phone_code_hash and client.session.save(), the half-authenticated StringSession, so the next step can resume the exact same MTProto session.
stepNotes.4: The browser holds an opaque token like 'gAAAAAB…FAKE'. It can't read or alter it; Fernet's HMAC rejects any change. That replaces a server-side pending-logins table.
stepNotes.5: _read_ticket(ticket, 'code') decrypts with the 600 s TTL and requires awaiting=='code'. On SessionPasswordNeededError it returns a new ticket with awaiting='password'. Replaying a code ticket at /password fails with LoginStateError.
stepNotes.6: One commit: a users row (telegram_user_id, phone, username, Argon2 password_hash, is_verified), and a storage_accounts row for Telegram with encrypted_credentials = Fernet(session), status 'connected', and a label. A username taken meanwhile falls back to the setup screen.
stepNotes.7: Access: HS256 JWT {sub, type:'access', iat, exp, jti}, 15 min, kept in memory. Refresh: token_urlsafe(48), 30 days. The raw token rides in an httpOnly cookie; the database keeps only its SHA-256. Each refresh revokes the old row; a reused revoked token gets 401.

nodeNotes.web-app: register/page.tsx walks Details → Code → Verify, holding only the opaque ticket between steps. It validates password length and match locally, and the code box accepts one-time-code autofill.
nodeNotes.auth-service: auth/telegram.py: start_signup, verify_code, verify_password, _complete. It builds and reads Fernet tickets, enforces the awaiting state, then creates the account and session.
nodeNotes.telegram: MTProto: send_code_request issues the code; sign_in proves the phone; get_me supplies the stable telegram_user_id that keys the BYOS account.
nodeNotes.postgres: Written only at the end: users, the Telegram storage_accounts row with the encrypted session, and a hashed refresh_tokens row. Nothing is written for abandoned sign-ups.

features.name: Log in two ways
features.summary: Password or Telegram code. Dead Telegram sessions get caught at the door.
features.description: Two tabs: password, or a Telegram code. Logging in with a code adds a device, a password doesn't. If you ended your Telegram sessions, the password login spots it and sends a fresh code instead.
features.underTheHood: Checking a password needs nothing from Telegram, so you could land in an account whose storage is dead. So after the Argon2 check, BYOS calls telegram_session_alive. If the session is gone, you get a code instead of a session.

steps.label: username + password
steps.narration: You type your username or phone, and your password.

steps.label: sends credentials
steps.narration: Rate-limited to 20 tries a minute per IP, for the optimists.

steps.label: checks password
steps.narration: Argon2 compares what you typed against the stored hash.

steps.label: is session alive?
steps.narration: If you ended your Telegram sessions, BYOS notices here and sends a fresh code instead.

steps.label: session or code
steps.narration: You either get your tokens, or a code and a polite note saying Telegram logged you out.

deep.algorithm: Password check plus live storage-session probe
deep.idea: A password login also checks that the Telegram session behind the account still works, and switches to a code login if it doesn't.
how: authenticate_password matches the lowercased username or the exact phone, with one generic failure message.
verify_password checks Argon2; needs_rehash upgrades stale hashes in place.
telegram_session_alive decrypts the stored session, connects and calls is_user_authorized().
Dead session: mark the storage expired, send an OTP, and return code_sent instead of tokens.
deep.why: Password login never touches Telegram, so a user who ended sessions in Telegram would otherwise get into an account whose files can't be opened.
deep.cost: One Telegram connect per password login.

stepNotes.3: Lookup by lowercased username OR exact phone. verify_password runs Argon2. If needs_rehash() says the stored hash uses old parameters, it's re-hashed with the current ones and saved, invisibly to the user.
stepNotes.4: telegram_session_alive decrypts the stored session, connects and calls is_user_authorized(). Any failure counts as dead: mark the storage 'expired', send an OTP to the saved phone, and return {status:'code_sent', ticket} instead of tokens.

nodeNotes.web-app: login/page.tsx Password tab. A code_sent response switches the UI to the code step with a 'Telegram access was logged out' notice.
nodeNotes.auth-service: login_password: authenticate_password, then telegram_session_alive. Alive issues a session; dead marks the storage expired and starts an OTP to the saved phone.
nodeNotes.postgres: users lookup by username or phone; Argon2 hash rehashed in place when parameters are outdated; storage_accounts status set to 'expired' on a dead session.
nodeNotes.telegram: Asked only is_user_authorized() with the stored session, a cheap probe of whether the auth key is still valid.

features.name: Uploads to your storage
features.summary: Drop files in. Bytes go to your storage; BYOS keeps the receipts.
features.description: Pick files or drag them in. They upload 3 at a time with a progress tray. Over 2 GB? Rejected in the browser. Upload the same file twice into one folder and you still get one copy.
features.underTheHood: The browser uses XMLHttpRequest because fetch has no upload progress events. The server checks everything first, then streams 1 MiB chunks to your storage, hashing as it goes. The file and its first version are saved in one commit, and if that fails the stored object is deleted.

steps.label: drops files
steps.narration: Three upload workers start, and each file gets its own row in the tray.

steps.label: file over XHR
steps.narration: The tray percentage comes straight from the upload's progress events.

steps.label: validates first
steps.narration: Size and folder checks happen before a single byte moves anywhere.

steps.label: streams the bytes
steps.narration: Bytes flow through in 1 MiB chunks, using your decrypted storage credentials.

steps.label: sends to Saved Messages
steps.narration: Your file becomes a message to yourself in Telegram. BYOS just keeps the message id.

steps.label: file + version rows
steps.narration: Same file already here? The new copy gets deleted, otherwise the rows go in with one commit.

steps.label: the new file
steps.narration: The file pops into the list if you're still looking at that folder.

deep.algorithm: Stream, hash, store, then idempotent commit
deep.idea: Bytes stream straight to the user's storage while being hashed; only then is the database touched, and both sides are kept consistent.
how: Validate first: folder ownership, size cap, blocked extensions, scan hook, then pick the target storage.
Stream 1 MiB reads to the provider, which buffers to disk and computes SHA-256 on the way.
The provider returns an opaque locator plus size and checksum.
If (owner, folder, name, hash) exists, delete the new object and return the old row.
Otherwise insert File + FileVersion and set current_version_id in one commit; on failure delete the object.
deep.why: The hash only exists after the stream is read, so dedup has to happen after storing. Cleaning up on both paths means retries never pile up copies or orphans.
deep.cost: One full disk buffer per upload; O(size) hashing.

stepNotes.2: XMLHttpRequest exposes upload.onprogress for real percentages; fetch has no upload-progress events. The dashboard runs 3 workers pulling from a shared job list, so 20 files never open 20 simultaneous multi-gigabyte connections.
stepNotes.3: Order: folder belongs to the user (404) → size ≤ MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES (413) → extension not blocked (400) → scan_upload clean (422) → resolve_upload_target (409/400). All checks run before the first byte reaches the provider.
stepNotes.4: file.read(1 MiB) chunks feed an async generator into provider.upload. Telegram writes them to a NamedTemporaryFile while updating SHA-256; GitHub and S3 spool (8 MB in memory, then disk) because they need the length first.
stepNotes.5: Returns StoredObjectRef{provider, locator:{chat:'me', message_id:123}, size, checksum}. The locator is opaque JSON. Telegram file_ids expire, but a message id doesn't, so a fresh file reference is fetched on each download.
stepNotes.6: Query (owner, folder, name, hash). Match: delete the just-stored object and return the existing row. Else flush File, flush FileVersion #1, set current_version_id, commit. Any exception rolls back and deletes the stored object.

nodeNotes.web-app: runJobs: a 3-worker pool over the upload queue. Each job uses XMLHttpRequest for progress; finished files are inserted into the list in place.
nodeNotes.api-gateway: Resolves the Bearer token to a Principal and enforces the files scope and per-key rate limit before the upload handler runs.
nodeNotes.metadata-engine: upload_file: validation, storage choice, streaming to the provider, then the dedup check, the single commit and orphan cleanup.
nodeNotes.storage-layer: StorageProvider.upload for the chosen backend. Hashes while buffering and returns an opaque StoredObjectRef; errors are tagged with the account id.
nodeNotes.telegram: Stores the bytes as a document in Saved Messages, named after the file, and returns a message id that never expires.
nodeNotes.postgres: files and file_versions inserted together, with current_version_id pointing at version 1, all in one transaction.

features.name: GitHub as storage
features.summary: Your files become release assets in a GitHub repo BYOS makes.
features.description: Paste a GitHub token, name a repo and pick private or public. BYOS creates it, or reuses one you can push to. Files up to 2 GB each go there, and the card shows when the token expires.
features.underTheHood: Files go in as release assets instead of commits. Commits cap at 100 MB and clog the history forever; assets take 2 GB and actually delete. Each UTC day gets its own prerelease, which keeps BYOS under GitHub's 1,000-assets-per-release limit.

steps.label: pastes token
steps.narration: You paste a token and name a repo. The button stays off until the token looks like one.

steps.label: sends token + repo
steps.narration: Only a logged-in session can do this. API keys need not apply.

steps.label: checks token, makes repo
steps.narration: BYOS checks who the token belongs to, then finds the repo or creates it, private unless you said otherwise.

steps.label: encrypted token
steps.narration: The token is stored encrypted. Reconnecting the same repo revives the old row instead of making a twin.

steps.label: storage card
steps.narration: The card shows the repo, whether it's private, usage and when the token expires.

keyFiles: apps/api/src/byos_api/storage/github.py — connect, daily releases, asset upload/download

deep.algorithm: Daily prerelease buckets of release assets
deep.idea: Files live as release assets, not commits, grouped into one prerelease per day.
how: connect: GET /user (reads the token expiry header), then reuse or create the repo with auto_init.
_release_id finds or creates prerelease byos-YYYY-MM-DD and caches its id per (repo, day).
Upload spools the stream to learn size and SHA-256, then POSTs to uploads.github.com.
The locator stores asset and release ids; downloads follow GitHub's redirect to a signed URL.
deep.why: Committed files cap at 100 MB, bloat history and are never truly deleted. Assets go to 2 GB and really disappear. Daily releases stay under 1,000 assets each.
deep.cost: One extra lookup per new day, then cached.

stepNotes.3: Missing repo → POST /user/repos {private, auto_init:true}, since releases need a commit to tag. Uploads go to prerelease byos-YYYY-MM-DD, staying under 1,000 assets per release. Assets hold 2 GB (commits cap at 100 MB) and are truly deletable.

nodeNotes.web-app: Connect sheet: token, repo name (default byos-storage), private toggle. The button enables at 10+ characters; reconnecting pre-fills the repo.
nodeNotes.storage-layer: github.connect checks the token and repo; GitHubStorageProvider spools uploads, picks today's release and maps HTTP errors to ProviderAuthError or ProviderError.
nodeNotes.github: Holds the repo (private by default) with daily prereleases of assets, and reports the token's expiry in a response header that BYOS records.
nodeNotes.postgres: storage_accounts row with the Fernet-encrypted token and {owner, repo, private, token_expires_at}. Reconnecting the same repo revives the old row so files reattach.

features.name: Storage usage and alerts
features.summary: See what each storage holds, and hear about dead keys early.
features.description: The sidebar shows how much each storage holds. A banner warns when a GitHub token expires within 14 days, or when keys stopped working and those files can't open. New uploads go to your default storage meanwhile.
features.underTheHood: When GitHub or S3 rejects your keys, the adapter raises a typed error and the API's error handler flags that storage as expired, then returns a 409 with a proper error code. The browser fires an event and the Drive reloads its storage list. Telegram never gets this treatment, since it's also your login.

steps.label: opens a file
steps.narration: You open a file that lives on a storage whose keys were revoked.

steps.label: keys get rejected
steps.narration: S3 says that access key doesn't exist anymore. Rude, but informative.

steps.label: flags as expired
steps.narration: That storage gets marked expired, so nobody has to find out the hard way twice.

steps.label: 409 + error code
steps.narration: The error names the provider and the account, so the app knows exactly which one broke.

steps.label: Reconnect banner
steps.narration: The banner and sidebar card switch to Reconnect, with the right form one click away.

deep.algorithm: Typed provider errors flag one storage
deep.idea: When a provider rejects credentials, only that storage is marked broken, and the client is told exactly which one.
how: Adapters raise ProviderAuthError(revoked=True) only when the credentials themselves are dead.
@tags_account stamps the account id onto the error on its way out.
The global handler calls flag_rejected on its own session, setting status 'expired'.
It returns 409 {code, provider, account_id}; the client fires 'byos:storage-rejected' and reloads storages.
deep.why: A generic 500 hid which storage failed. Telegram gets a separate code because it is also the login: the fix there is to sign in again, not reconnect.

stepNotes.2: S3's InvalidAccessKeyId (or GitHub 401) becomes ProviderAuthError(revoked=True). AccessDenied stays revoked=False: the keys work but lack a permission, so the storage isn't flagged as dead.
stepNotes.3: @tags_account stamped the account id on the error. flag_rejected opens its own SessionLocal, because the request's session may be mid-transaction or already closed, and sets status='expired'.
stepNotes.4: 409 {code:'storage_credentials_rejected', provider:'s3', account_id:'…'}. useAuthed dispatches 'byos:storage-rejected' and the Drive reloads storages. Telegram returns 'telegram_session_expired' instead, since it's also the login: the user must sign in again.

nodeNotes.web-app: useAuthed sees code storage_credentials_rejected and fires 'byos:storage-rejected'. The Drive reloads storages; storage-alert.tsx and the sidebar switch that storage to Reconnect.
nodeNotes.storage-layer: Translates provider errors: dead keys become ProviderAuthError(revoked=True); missing permissions stay revoked=False. @tags_account adds the account id.
nodeNotes.s3: Answers InvalidAccessKeyId, SignatureDoesNotMatch or ExpiredToken when keys are dead, and AccessDenied when keys lack a permission.
nodeNotes.postgres: storage_accounts.status flips to 'expired' via flag_rejected on a separate session, so the flag survives even if the request transaction rolls back.
nodeNotes.api-gateway: The global ProviderAuthError handler returns 409 with code, provider and account_id; Telegram gets 'telegram_session_expired' instead.

features.name: Version history
features.summary: Replace a file and keep every old version around.
features.description: Upload a new version and the old ones stay listed with their size and time. Any older one can be restored instantly or downloaded. The current version can't be deleted, and replacing with identical content does nothing.
features.underTheHood: Telegram can't edit a message in place, so the storage layer has no replace at all. A replace uploads fresh bytes, adds version N+1 and moves the current-version pointer in one transaction. Restoring an old version only moves the pointer.

steps.label: picks new file
steps.narration: You hit Replace in the Versions dialog and pick the new file.

steps.label: uploads replacement
steps.narration: It goes to the same storage the file already lives on.

steps.label: stores new object
steps.narration: Telegram can't edit a message, so a 'replace' is secretly a brand new message and a pointer swap.

steps.label: moves the pointer
steps.narration: Same content changes nothing. Otherwise it gets a new version number and the pointer moves to it.

steps.label: version list
steps.narration: Older versions sit in the list, ready to be restored or deleted.

deep.algorithm: Immutable versions plus a movable pointer
deep.idea: Every upload is a new immutable row; the file just points at whichever version is current.
how: file_versions rows never change; (file_id, version_no) is unique.
Replace uploads new bytes; the same hash as current is a no-op.
Otherwise insert version N+1 and move files.current_version_id in one commit.
Restore only moves the pointer; the current version can't be deleted (409).
deep.example:
v1(a1f…) ← current
replace → v2(b7c…) ← current
restore v1 → pointer = v1, v2 kept
deep.why: Telegram messages and release assets can't be edited, so 'replace' as a provider operation is impossible. A pointer flip works the same on every backend and keeps links stable.
deep.cost: Restore is O(1); storage grows per version.

stepNotes.4: Before: v1 ← current_version_id. Replace with a new hash: insert v2, pointer → v2. Same hash: nothing. Restore v1: pointer → v1, v2 untouched. Rows never mutate, which is why the provider protocol has no replace().

nodeNotes.web-app: versions-modal.tsx lists versions with a 'current' badge; restore and delete apply to older ones only. Replace reports that the link now opens the new version.
nodeNotes.metadata-engine: replace_file uploads to the file's existing storage, compares the hash with the current version, then inserts the next version_no and moves the pointer.
nodeNotes.storage-layer: Creates a brand-new object per version (message, asset or key); old objects stay until their version is deleted.
nodeNotes.postgres: file_versions (immutable, unique version_no) plus files.current_version_id. Restoring repoints that and copies the version's size and hash onto the file row.

features.name: Nested folders
features.summary: Folders inside folders inside folders, with breadcrumbs so you don't get lost.
features.description: Folders nest as deep as you like and show their total size. Drag one onto another to move it, but not into itself, nice try. Deleting a folder takes everything inside it and runs in the background.
features.underTheHood: Folders are a plain parent_id list. Breadcrumbs and the can't-move-into-yourself check are recursive SQL queries. Deleting walks the whole subtree and removes every file's bytes from your storage before the records go, so nothing is left lying around.

steps.label: deletes a folder
steps.narration: You confirm the delete. The folder vanishes from view right away.

steps.label: delete request
steps.narration: The real work runs in the background behind a red progress pill.

steps.label: walks the subtree
steps.narration: It collects every nested folder and every file inside them.

steps.label: deletes the bytes
steps.narration: Each file's versions are deleted from your storage first, so nothing gets orphaned.

steps.label: deletes messages
steps.narration: The Telegram messages go. On GitHub or S3 it's assets or objects instead.

steps.label: removes records
steps.narration: Only then do the folder rows go, and the subfolders follow by cascade.

keyFiles: apps/api/src/byos_api/folders/service.py — breadcrumb CTE, cycle check, subtree_sizes, delete_folder

deep.algorithm: Adjacency list with recursive CTEs
deep.idea: Folders store only their parent; recursive SQL walks up for breadcrumbs and down for subtrees.
how: folders.parent_id forms the tree; NULL is the root.
breadcrumb: a recursive CTE walks parent links upward, ordered by depth.
move_folder: a recursive CTE walks down from the folder; the target inside it means InvalidMove.
delete_folder: collect subtree ids, delete each file's bytes best-effort, then rows; subfolders cascade.
deep.example: move A into A/B/C → CTE from A finds C → 400 cycle
deep.why: An adjacency list makes moves O(1) row updates. Breadcrumbs and the cycle check are single recursive CTEs; subtree sweeps load the owner's folders once and walk them in memory.
deep.cost: Walks are O(depth) or O(subtree).

stepNotes.3: Collecting the subtree to delete: load the owner's (id, parent_id) pairs once and walk them in Python with a stack. The recursive SQL lives elsewhere: breadcrumbs walk up with a depth column, and move_folder's cycle check rejects moving A into A/B.
stepNotes.4: Bytes before records: deleting rows first and then failing at the provider would orphan files nobody can see. For a single file, a provider error aborts the delete so it stays retryable.
stepNotes.5: Telegram delete_messages(chat, [message_id]). Deleting a message that's already gone is a no-op, so retries are safe. MESSAGE_DELETE_FORBIDDEN becomes a readable ProviderError.
stepNotes.6: Inside a folder delete, byte removal is best-effort: one provider hiccup is logged and the walk continues, so a recursive delete can't strand halfway. Then file rows go, and subfolders cascade through the parent_id foreign key.

nodeNotes.web-app: Hides the folder immediately and runs the delete in the background with a 'Deleting n/total' pill; failures produce one summary toast and a resync.
nodeNotes.metadata-engine: folders/service.py: recursive-CTE breadcrumb and cycle check, subtree_folder_ids, and delete_folder's bytes-then-records walk.
nodeNotes.postgres: Adjacency list (parent_id, ON DELETE CASCADE). Recursive CTEs handle breadcrumbs and the move cycle check; deleting the root folder cascades to its subfolders.
nodeNotes.storage-layer: delete_file_bytes deletes every version's object. Raises for single-file deletes; wrapped as best-effort inside folder deletes.
nodeNotes.telegram: delete_messages removes the stored documents; deleting already-gone messages is a harmless no-op.

features.name: Missing-file scan
features.summary: Deleted something straight from Telegram? BYOS finds the leftovers.
features.description: Your files live in your own storage, so you can delete them there behind BYOS's back. The Missing page lists those and when they vanished, and Scan now rechecks everything. Then you clean up the dead records.
features.underTheHood: Each provider has a cheap exists() check that downloads nothing. A scan runs it over every file and flags or un-flags them. Files also get flagged when someone opens one and the provider shrugs. If Telegram says slow down, the scan stops early.

steps.label: Scan now
steps.narration: You hit Scan now and get an honest progress bar that has no idea how long this takes.

steps.label: verify request
steps.narration: Every file with a current version gets checked.

steps.label: asks: still there?
steps.narration: Each provider checks whether the object exists, without downloading it.

steps.label: looks up messages
steps.narration: A deleted message means a missing file. If Telegram says slow down, the scan stops early.

steps.label: flags missing files
steps.narration: Missing files get flagged, and any that came back get un-flagged.

steps.label: the missing list
steps.narration: Each row says when it went missing, with buttons to remove the records.

deep.algorithm: Lazy flagging plus a cheap existence scan
deep.idea: Find bytes deleted outside BYOS, either when someone hits one or by asking every provider cheaply.
how: stream_object's on_missing sets files.missing_at when a provider says the object is gone.
verify_missing loops current versions and calls provider.exists(), which downloads nothing.
It sets or clears missing_at per file and returns {checked, missing}.
FloodWait stops early with partial counts; a dead session re-raises.
deep.why: The database can't know about deletes made directly in Telegram, GitHub or S3. Existence checks are cheap; downloads would be prohibitive.
deep.cost: One provider call per file; sequential.

stepNotes.3: Telegram: get_messages(chat, ids=message_id), missing if None or no media. S3: head_object, 404 means missing. GitHub: GET the asset metadata, 404 means missing. None downloads the bytes.
stepNotes.4: Telethon's FloodWaitError breaks the loop: the scan commits what it checked and returns partial {checked, missing} rather than failing. A dead session (ProviderAuthError) is re-raised so the user is asked to sign in.
stepNotes.5: Lazy: any download that hits FileNotFoundError calls on_missing and sets missing_at, at no extra cost. Bulk: /files/verify also clears missing_at for files that came back.

nodeNotes.web-app: missing-panel.tsx runs the scan with an indeterminate bar, lists flagged files with 'Gone since', and offers Remove record and Remove all.
nodeNotes.metadata-engine: verify_missing walks files with a current version, calls exists() per file, updates missing_at both ways and stops early on FloodWait.
nodeNotes.storage-layer: exists() per adapter: Telegram message lookup, S3 head_object, GitHub asset metadata. No bytes are read.
nodeNotes.telegram: get_messages by message id: None or no media means the bytes were deleted directly in Telegram.
nodeNotes.postgres: files.missing_at timestamp: set when gone, cleared when back. DELETE /files/missing removes only these records.

features.name: Search operators
features.summary: Type type:pdf size:>2mb, or just 'pdfs from last week'.
features.description: Filters for type, size, tags, folder, dates and starred files, plus quoted phrases and -exclude. Or type like a human: 'pdfs from last week larger than 2mb'. Whatever's left over is fuzzy-matched against file names. Tags only match through tag:.
features.underTheHood: One regex tokenises the query and pulls out the operators and plain-English bits. What's left goes to Postgres: a full-text search vector, plus a trigram index so half-typed words still match. Results are ranked and capped at 50 (the API would allow 100).

steps.label: types a query
steps.narration: Something like 'pdfs from last week >2mb invoice'.

steps.label: search request
steps.narration: API keys can search too, if they have read access to files.

steps.label: parses the query
steps.narration: That becomes a PDF filter, a date range, a minimum size, and the word 'invoice'.

steps.label: full-text + trigram
steps.narration: Filters run in SQL, then results are ranked by how well they match.

keyFiles: apps/api/alembic/versions/0001_initial.py — pg_trgm, generated search_vector, GIN indexes

deep.algorithm: Operator parser plus full-text and trigram SQL
deep.idea: Turn a typed query into structured filters plus leftover words, then let Postgres filter and rank.
how: One regex splits tokens into key:value, "phrase" or bare words.
Known operators fill ParsedQuery; unknown key:value pairs stay text.
The natural-language fallback reads size and recency phrases and type words, without overriding operators.
SQL: filters AND (search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery OR name ILIKE), ordered by ts_rank then newest.
deep.example:
"pdfs from last week >2mb invoice"
→ ext=pdf, since_days=7, min_size=2097152, text='invoice'
→ WHERE ext='pdf' AND size>=2097152
  AND created_at>=now()-7d AND (fts OR ILIKE)
deep.why: A rule parser is free, instant and predictable; the docstring notes an LLM parser could replace parse() behind the same contract.
deep.cost: GIN indexes cover the text match; filters are plain columns.

stepNotes.3: "pdfs from last week >2mb invoice": '>2mb' isn't an operator, so the natural-language fallback reads size (≥2,097,152 bytes), 'last week' (7 days), and 'pdfs' (ext=pdf), dropping stop-words. Result: ParsedQuery{ext:'pdf', min_size:2097152, since_days:7, text:'invoice'}.
stepNotes.4: search_vector = to_tsvector('english', name||ext||mime), a generated column with a GIN index. Match: @@ websearch_to_tsquery OR name ILIKE (trigram GIN index). Order: ts_rank DESC, created_at DESC. Tags filter separately via file_tags.

deep.algorithm: Indirection: slug → file → current version
deep.idea: A link names a logical file, not bytes, so replacing the file changes what the link serves.
how: aliases rows: unique (owner, slug); exactly one of file_id or folder_id.
resolve: username → alias → file → current_version_id → FileVersion.
stream_object reads the first chunk before sending headers, then streams inline.
ETag = version hash; a matching If-None-Match returns 304 without touching the provider.
deep.example:
GET /demo-user/resume  If-None-Match: "a1f…"
current hash b7c… ≠ a1f… → 200, ETag "b7c…"
repeat → 304
deep.why: The catch-all /{username}/{slug} is registered last because FastAPI matches in order: registered earlier, it would capture two-segment API paths like /analytics/overview.
deep.cost: About five indexed lookups per hit (user, alias, file, version, storage account), and a 304 pays for them too.

stepNotes.3: CHECK num_nonnulls(file_id, folder_id) = 1; UNIQUE(owner_id, slug); partial unique indexes on (owner_id, file_id) and (owner_id, folder_id). Slugs must match ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,127}$, e.g. 'resume-2026'.
stepNotes.5: Alias → file → current version. If If-None-Match equals the version hash → 304. Otherwise read the first chunk before sending headers, so a missing object returns 404, not a broken 200. Then stream inline with ETag.

deep.algorithm: In-memory subtree set for access control
deep.idea: A shared folder grants access to exactly its descendants, checked by building the set of allowed folder ids.
how: API URL for a folder alias → 302 to WEB_BASE_URL/{user}/{slug}.
_subtree_folder_ids loads (id, parent_id) for the owner and builds a parent→children map.
A depth-first walk from the shared root collects every descendant id into a set.
Any requested folder_id or file's folder_id outside the set → 404.
deep.why: Per-user folder counts are small, so one query plus a walk in memory is simpler than a recursive query per request. 404 instead of 403 doesn't confirm that folders outside the share exist.
deep.cost: O(owner's folders) per public request.

stepNotes.3: resolve() sees folder_id set and raises NotAFolderAlias; the route answers 302 → {WEB_BASE_URL}/{username}/{slug}. Folder links are pages, not downloads, so the API redirects to the web app.
stepNotes.5: _subtree_folder_ids: SELECT id, parent_id for the owner; build children[parent] lists; walk a stack from the shared root, adding ids to a set. A requested folder_id outside the set → 404.
stepNotes.6: public_file_in_share checks file.folder_id ∈ subtree before streaming. Guessing another file's id from the same owner fails. A 404 rather than 403 avoids confirming the file exists.

deep.algorithm: Chunk, embed, cache per file version and model
deep.idea: Each file version is turned into overlapping text chunks, embedded with the user's model, and cached until the file changes or goes unused.
how: Resolve targets; skip files already embedded for (current version, model) before downloading.
Download (≤25 MB), extract text: pypdf per page, text decode, vision for sparse pages.
chunk_text: 1,800-char windows, 200 overlap, ending at a paragraph, line or sentence break when it sits past halfway.
Embed in batches of 64; delete old (file, model) chunks; insert REAL[] rows.
Retry 429s three times; a bad key stops the run; other errors skip the file.
deep.why: Caching by version and model means unchanged files never re-embed, while replacing a file or switching models invalidates exactly what changed. last_used_at expiry reclaims space nobody searches.
deep.cost: One embedding call per 64 chunks; one download per changed file.

stepNotes.2: _index_targets gathers all, picked files, or picked folders' files, keeping extractable ones. Per file, is_embedded(file, current_version, model) returns before any download if chunks exist, unless force is set.
stepNotes.3: _extract_owned downloads up to 25 MB. PDFs: pypdf per page, encrypted ones tried with an empty password. Text: about 40 extensions plus text/*, JSON, XML and JS MIME types, UTF-8 with replacement. Read cap 2,000,000 chars; embed cap 1.5 M.
stepNotes.4:
chunk_text(size=1800, overlap=200): a window ends at the last '

', '
' or '. ' if that's past char 900, otherwise at 1,800. Next start = end − 200. A 4,000-char doc gives about 3 chunks. Then batches of 64.
stepNotes.5: LLMRateLimited and LLMUnreachable retry 3 times, waiting Retry-After or 2/4/8 s, capped at 30 s. LLMAuthError stops the whole run: every remaining file would fail with the same bad key.
stepNotes.6: ensure_embedded deletes old (file, model) chunks, then inserts {file_id, version_id, embed_model, chunk_index, content, embedding REAL[]}. Any dimension fits. Searches update last_used_at; a daily loop deletes chunks idle for 30 days.

deep.algorithm: Selective page OCR via a multimodal LLM
deep.idea: Only pages with no real text layer are rendered to images and transcribed by the user's model.
how: pdf_pages returns per-page text; empty pages come back as ''.
sparse_pages picks pages under 80 chars.
Render those at 2× with pypdfium2 in a worker thread, at most 20 per file.
Each PNG goes to the model at temperature 0; the first refusal stops the loop.
deep.example:
pages: [1,840 chars, 12 chars, 0 chars]
sparse → [1, 2] → 2 vision calls
page 1 text kept as is
deep.why: Sending every page would charge for text already extractable. Stopping at the first refusal avoids paying N times for a model that can't see images.
deep.cost: One vision call per scanned page, capped at 20.

stepNotes.4: sparse_pages keeps indexes with fewer than 80 chars, e.g. [1, 2]. _render loads the PDF in pypdfium2, renders those pages at scale 2.0 (about 144 DPI) as PNG in a worker thread, at most AI_VISION_MAX_PAGES = 20.

deep.algorithm: Tool-calling agent over vector-ranked excerpts
deep.idea: The model decides what to look up, gets excerpts back as tool results, and answers with verifiable citations.
how: Loop: chat_tools call → run READ tools → append results as role 'tool' messages.
search_content embeds the query. Postgres ranks chunks by pgvector cosine distance and returns the top 40, and _diversify cuts that to k (8 by default), one chunk per file first.
Stop when the model replies without tool calls, calls ask_user, or hits MAX_STEPS.
citations.split strips [source:] lines; pick verifies quotes; events stream \x1e-framed.
deep.why: Letting the model choose searches handles multi-hop questions that one retrieval pass misses. Non-streamed steps keep tool calls intact; the client fakes typing for the final answer.
deep.cost: One model call per round, up to 10.

stepNotes.3: Up to MAX_STEPS=10 rounds of llm.chat_tools (non-streamed, at least 8,192 tokens). It stops on no tool calls (that's the answer), ask_user, finish_reason 'length' (error), or steps exhausted. Streaming is skipped because providers fragment tool-call deltas differently.
stepNotes.4: search_content returns {hits:[{file_id, name, excerpt}]}: 8 by default, up to 20, each excerpt ≤1,500 chars. It's appended as a role 'tool' message (JSON capped at 20,000 chars), which is how excerpts reach the model.
stepNotes.5: The query is embedded once. Postgres orders the user's chunks for that model by embedding::vector <=> CAST(:q AS real[])::vector and returns the top 40, using the (user_id, embed_model) index. _diversify then keeps 8, each file's best chunk first. Exact cosine distance via pgvector; only those 40 rows leave the database.

features.summary: Four optional tricks for better search, each costing at least one extra model call.
features.description: In the + menu: rewrite the question, search with a draft answer (HyDE), rerank results, and retry weak searches. Each one costs at least one extra model call. They're all off until you turn them on.

steps.narration: The rewritten question, or the draft answer, gets embedded, and pgvector ranks your chunks right inside Postgres.

steps.narration: The model reorders the hits and grades the top 4. A NO means one more search.

deep.algorithm: Rewrite, HyDE, rerank, corrective retry, diversify
deep.idea: Optional LLM passes around vector search fix the main failure modes: vague wording, vocabulary mismatch, bad order, and weak results.
how: Rewrite: the model turns the question into a keyword query.
HyDE: the model writes a plausible answer passage; that passage is embedded instead.
Retrieve 40 candidates; Rerank: the model lists the best snippet indices.
CRAG: YES/NO on the top 4; NO triggers one rewritten re-search.
_diversify: each file's best chunk first, then the rest, cut to keep.
deep.why: Each pass costs a model call, so each is a toggle, not a default. Every pass fails safe: a failed call falls back to the plain path instead of erroring.
deep.cost: Up to 6 extra small calls per search (512 tokens, temperature 0.1) when every add-on is on and the retry kicks in.

stepNotes.4: Rewrite sends 'Rewrite into a keyword-rich search query' and gets e.g. 'june 2026 payslip net pay'. HyDE sends 'Write a plausible passage that answers it' and embeds that passage. Both use temperature 0.1, max_tokens 512, falling back on error.
stepNotes.6: Rerank lists [i] (file) snippet[:500] and parses the returned indices, best first. CRAG asks YES/NO on the top 4 snippets. NO → rewrite again, search again, and rerank again if on. A grading error counts as YES.
stepNotes.7: Hits [A1, A2, B1, C1], keep 3 → primary (first per file) [A1, B1, C1] + extras [A2] → [A1, B1, C1]. Without this, a file with two strong chunks could push out a third document.

deep.algorithm: Model-declared quotes checked by substring
deep.idea: The model names its sources with exact quotes; the server keeps only quotes that really appear in text the agent read.
how: The prompt asks for one '[source: <file_id> | exact words]' line per file used.
split() regexes those lines out and strips a trailing 'Sources:' heading.
pick() drops ids the agent never read, then checks normalised quote ⊂ normalised file text.
Failing that, keep figures (3+ digits) from the quote that appear; with no citations, match the answer's figures.
deep.example:
read: payslip.pdf ("Total Net Pay ₹00,000.00")
cite "Total Net Pay ₹00,000.00" → kept
cite "net salary was 00k" → dropped
cite id never read → dropped
deep.why: Models paraphrase and sometimes invent ids. Checking substrings against text the agent actually read makes every highlight trustworthy without a second model call.
deep.cost: Linear string scans; no extra model call.

stepNotes.2: The prompt asks for one line per file actually used: '[source: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 | Total Net Pay ₹00,000.00]'. Words are copied exactly; for a figure, both figure and label. The user never sees these lines.
stepNotes.3: Normalise: collapse whitespace and lowercase. Read text contains 'total net pay ₹00,000.00': that quote is kept. 'Net salary was 00k' isn't a substring, so it falls back to its 3+ digit figures. An id never read is dropped.

deep.algorithm: Text-layer matching with overlay boxes
deep.idea: Render the PDF yourself, find the quote's words in pdf.js's text layer, and draw boxes over them.
how: Fetch metadata, then the content blob through the API.
pdf.js renders each page (≤40) to canvas and returns text items with positions.
Flatten text items to one lowercase string with collapsed spaces, each character traced to its item; find the quote, else its figures.
Per matched item, character offsets × average glyph width give a rectangle; tinted boxes overlay the canvas, first scrolled into view.
deep.why: The browser's built-in PDF viewer can't be told to highlight anything, and PDF text often breaks words oddly, so strict matching would miss.
deep.cost: Renders up to 40 pages client-side.

stepNotes.4: Flatten the page's text items into one string, lowercase with whitespace collapsed, tracing each character to its item. Find the quote; if absent, its 3+ digit figures. Turn covered character spans into boxes using each item's width ÷ length.

features.name: Permission modes
features.summary: Four levels of trust, from Bookish Bao to Boss Bao.
features.description: Read only (Bookish Bao) never changes anything. Ask first (Butler Bao) queues every change for you. Auto-organize (Busy Bao) does reversible stuff but waits on deletes and public links. Full access (Boss Bao) just does it.
features.underTheHood: One small function decides whether a write runs now: Full always, Auto only when it isn't dangerous, the others never. Deletes and share links count as dangerous. Read-only turns aren't even offered the write tools, so there's nothing to misuse.

steps.label: picks a mode
steps.narration: You tap the avatar and pick which Bao you're dealing with today.

steps.label: remembers the mode
steps.narration: Your choice is saved on this device, unless Settings pins a starting mode.

steps.label: mode in request
steps.narration: The mode rides along with every chat message.

steps.label: tools for mode
steps.narration: Read only gets read tools only. Other modes get write tools too, and every mode gets a short brief.

steps.label: runs or queues
steps.narration: Each write either runs now or waits in the plan, depending on the mode.

keyFiles: apps/web/lib/avatars.ts — Bao names and colours per mode
apps/web/components/mode-avatar.tsx — the SVG panda per mode

deep.algorithm: Two-input gate: mode × danger flag
deep.idea: Every write is either run now or queued, decided by the mode and whether the action is destructive or public.
how: Mode is sent per request; read_only removes write tools from the schema entirely.
Each Tool has danger=True for delete_file, delete_folder, create_share_link, create_alias.
runs_now: full → always; auto → if not danger; ask/read_only → never.
Each mode adds a matching brief to the system prompt.
deep.example:
auto + move_file(danger=False) → runs now
auto + delete_file(danger=True) → queued
ask + anything → queued
deep.why: A gradient lets users hand over trust gradually. Auto makes bulk tidying effortless while irreversible or public actions still need a click.

stepNotes.5: runs_now(mode, danger): full → True; auto → not danger; ask → False; read_only never sees write tools. danger=True: delete_file, delete_folder, create_share_link, create_alias. Safe: create_folder, move, rename, tag, star.

nodeNotes.web-app: mode-menu.tsx picks one of four modes and tints Bao's avatar; the composer border shows the mode's colour.
nodeNotes.browser-apis: localStorage 'byos:byok:mode' remembers the last mode; unknown stored values are ignored.
nodeNotes.bao-agent: Reads the mode: tool schemas without writes for read_only, the mode brief in the prompt, and runs_now for every write call.
nodeNotes.llm-client: Receives only the tools the mode allows, so a read-only model can't even attempt a write.
nodeNotes.metadata-engine: Executes writes that runs_now allows during the turn, through the same services as the REST API.

features.name: Plans you approve
features.summary: Bao drafts the changes. You press Apply, or you don't.
features.description: When Bao wants to change your drive, the reply ends in a plan card like '14 changes to confirm'. Permanent or public changes get a red warning. Apply runs the lot, and anything that fails shows why.
features.underTheHood: In Ask mode, write tools don't run. Bao records them and tells the model they're done, so it can chain 'make Finance, then move 12 files into it'. Apply loads the stored plan, never the browser's copy, and a double click can't run it twice.

steps.label: asks for changes
steps.narration: In Ask first mode: 'Move all my tax documents into one folder.'

steps.label: writes get queued
steps.narration: Each write is noted down and the model is told it worked. A small, useful lie.

steps.label: saves the plan
steps.narration: The plan is stored on the server, every action in order, waiting for you.

steps.label: plan card
steps.narration: The plan streams in and shows up as a card.

steps.label: presses Apply
steps.narration: Bao drafts the plan and touches nothing. You're the one holding the Apply button.

steps.label: apply request
steps.narration: Only a pending plan can run. New folders get made first, parents before children.

steps.label: runs each action
steps.narration: Each change goes through the same code as the regular API, ownership checks and all.

keyFiles: apps/web/components/byok/plan-card.tsx — card, apply, discard, failed filter, danger banner

deep.algorithm: Deferred writes with placeholders, stored server-side
deep.idea: Write tool calls become recorded actions; placeholders let later actions reference folders that don't exist yet.
how: A queued write gets {queued:true}; a queued create_folder returns folder_id '$new:N'.
Bad $new refs and duplicate folders are caught while planning.
save_plan stores actions plus a parallel result array; null means waiting.
apply: 409 unless pending; apply_order puts folders first; resolve $new; record per-action outcomes.
deep.example:
0 create_folder Finance → '$new:0'
1 move_file a.pdf → $new:0
2 move_file b.pdf → $new:0
apply: 0 → uuid…FAKE, then 1, 2
deep.why: Storing the plan means apply only runs what the model proposed, survives reloads, and a double click can't run it twice. Round-tripping actions through the client would allow tampering.

stepNotes.2: _ack returns {queued:true, note:'awaiting user confirmation'}; a queued create_folder also returns folder_id '$new:3' (its plan index). The model then calls move_file(folder_id='$new:3') as if the folder existed.
stepNotes.3: ai_action_plans: actions=[{op, args, label, danger, auto}], result=[outcome|null] at matching indexes. Any null hole → status 'pending'; otherwise 'applied'. Terminal states (applied, discarded) are never re-entered.
stepNotes.6: apply_plan loads the stored row, never client-sent actions, and returns 409 once the plan isn't pending; the Apply button also locks while it runs, which is what really stops a double click. Actions already done in Auto mode keep their outcome; only the null holes run.
stepNotes.7: apply_order: create_folders first, each after its $new parent, then everything else as listed. created[index] = real UUID resolves '$new:N'. Each failure rolls back that action only, is recorded, and the loop continues.

nodeNotes.web-app: plan-card.tsx shows actions, the danger banner, Apply, Discard and the failed filter; plan-tree.tsx draws the preview.
nodeNotes.bao-agent: Queues writes, issues $new refs, rejects bad refs and duplicate folders, saves the plan, and later applies it in dependency order.
nodeNotes.llm-client: The model keeps planning after each acknowledgement, chaining actions that depend on folders not yet created.
nodeNotes.postgres: ai_action_plans: actions JSONB, result JSONB with null holes, status pending/applied/discarded, applied_at.
nodeNotes.metadata-engine: Runs each action through the normal services, so ownership checks, folder cycle checks and tag normalisation still apply.

features.name: Revise in plain words
features.summary: Not quite right? Tell Bao, and the plan gets rewritten.
features.description: Under a pending plan, 'Want it different?' lets you type something like 'keep the tax files in their own folder'. The same message gets a new plan. If that fails, the old plan stays, still ready to apply.
features.underTheHood: The old plan goes back to the model along with a remove_change tool for dropping items. Dropping a folder also drops everything headed into it. The new plan is saved before the old one is retired, so a failed revision costs nothing.

steps.label: types a note
steps.narration: You say what's wrong. The card dims while an animated Bao walks along the rows.

steps.label: note + old plan
steps.narration: The server loads the old plan, checks it's yours, and hands it to the new run.

steps.label: edits the plan
steps.narration: The model keeps, adds or removes numbered changes.

steps.label: swaps the plan
steps.narration: The new plan is saved first. Only then is the old one retired.

steps.label: revised plan
steps.narration: The message swaps in one go, right after a small 'Done!' confetti moment.

deep.algorithm: Seeded replanning with cascading removal
deep.idea: The old plan is handed back to the agent with stable numbers, so it edits the plan instead of rewriting it.
how: Old actions seed the new run under their old indexes; previous_plan describes up to 300.
remove_change(n) marks drops; new writes append.
_without drops dependents transitively and renumbers $new refs.
The old plan is retired only after the new run finishes with a reply.
deep.example:
plan: 0 mkdir Tax, 1 move x → $new:0, 2 move y
remove_change(0) → also drops 1
kept: 2 (renumbered to 0)
deep.why: Rewriting a 200-change plan from scratch is slow and error-prone; dropping by number is precise and cheap.
deep.cost: One agent run, seeded.

stepNotes.3: remove_change(2) adds 2 to removed. _without loops until stable: any action whose args reference a dropped $new folder is dropped too. Survivors are re-indexed, so '$new:5' becomes '$new:3' when two earlier actions vanish.
stepNotes.4: _retire_plan (pending → discarded) runs only after agent.run finishes with an answer or plan. A failed or stopped revision never reaches it, so the old plan stays applicable. A plan applied meanwhile isn't touched.

nodeNotes.web-app: Sends revises=<planId> with the note, buffers the reply off-screen while Bao animates, then swaps the message in one step.
nodeNotes.bao-agent: Seeds the run with the old actions, offers remove_change, and filters the result through _without.
nodeNotes.llm-client: The model gets the numbered previous plan and the note, and replies with removals and additions only.
nodeNotes.postgres: The new plan is saved and the old one marked discarded only after success; the chat message is rewritten in place with 'You asked:' on top.

features.name: /organize the drive
features.summary: One command to tidy the whole drive, or just ask nicely.
features.description: Type /organize to pick a grouping and how deep folders go, plus whether to rename or tag. Or just say 'clean up my receipts'. Defaults are cautious: your names and folders stay as they are.
features.underTheHood: BYOS spots tidy-up requests by matching a verb like 'declutter' with a thing like 'downloads'. The run gets an inventory of up to 600 files and 30 steps. Delete and share tools are never offered, so a cleanup can't turn into a purge.

steps.label: /organize
steps.narration: A settings panel opens with cautious defaults. Enter starts it.

steps.label: request + options
steps.narration: The message goes out with your chosen options attached.

steps.label: lists your files
steps.narration: Up to 600 files, with their paths, go into Bao's brief.

steps.label: plans the moves
steps.narration: Bao can read inside files, so scan_0032.pdf still ends up in the right folder.

steps.label: plan + diagram
steps.narration: The plan comes back with a tree of what the drive will look like after.

deep.algorithm: Intent regex plus constrained agent run
deep.idea: Detect tidy-up requests, give the agent a full inventory and only the tools the settings allow.
how: looks_like_organizing: a verb regex (organize, tidy, clean up…) AND an object regex (files, downloads, receipts…).
inventory: up to 600 files with folder paths, appended to the task with brief(settings).
excluded_tools always removes delete, share, alias and favourite; renames and tags only when enabled.
Every organizing run gets MAX_STEPS = 30, including plain requests like 'clean up my receipts'. Normal turns get 10.
deep.example:
"clean up my receipts" → verb 'clean up' + object 'receipts'
→ OrganizeOptions(rename=False, tags=False, group_by='auto')
deep.why: Withholding tools enforces the settings structurally, not by asking the model nicely. A cheap regex avoids a classifier call.
deep.cost: Inventory adds up to 600 lines of prompt.

stepNotes.2: Lowercase, then both must hit: _VERB (organi[sz]e|tidy|clean ?up|sort out|declutter…) and _THING (files?|drive|downloads|receipts|payslips…). 'tidy my downloads' matches; 'tidy answer please' doesn't. Rename and tags turn on only if those words appear.
stepNotes.3: organize.inventory lists every folder as 'id: path' and up to INVENTORY_MAX = 600 files as 'id | name | folder | type' lines, plus a note to page list_files for the rest. Appended with organize.brief(settings), saving tool rounds.
stepNotes.4: excluded_tools always removes delete_file, delete_folder, create_share_link, create_alias and set_favorite. rename_file goes unless rename is on; tag tools unless tags; folder moves and renames under keep_existing; content reads if 'Look inside files' is off. MAX_STEPS = 30.

nodeNotes.web-app: organize-panel.tsx or lib/organize.ts arguments build OrganizeOptions; Read-only mode asks before switching to Ask first.
nodeNotes.bao-agent: Detects intent, appends inventory and brief, sets excluded_tools and MAX_STEPS = 30, then runs the normal plan flow.
nodeNotes.metadata-engine: organize.inventory reads up to 600 files with their folder paths for the prompt.
nodeNotes.llm-client: Only receives tool schemas the settings allow, so excluded actions are impossible rather than discouraged.

features.name: Model compatibility check
features.summary: BYOS learns what each model accepts, so weird providers still work.
features.description: Pick a model and BYOS runs a quick check, greying out settings it refuses and listing the reasoning levels it supports. Results are cached in your browser. If a provider still rejects something mid-chat, BYOS fixes the request and retries.
features.underTheHood: The check sends one tiny 'ping' and notes every parameter the provider rejects. OpenRouter never complains, so there BYOS reads its model list instead. Mid-chat, a 400 gets read, the bad parameter is dropped or renamed, and the fix is remembered per model. Supported reasoning levels are scraped straight from the error message.

steps.label: picks a model
steps.narration: The form checks the browser cache first. On a miss it waits 600 ms, then asks the server.

steps.label: check request
steps.narration: BYOS sends one tiny probe request to the model.

steps.label: probe request
steps.narration: If the provider complains about a parameter, the probe tries again without it.

steps.label: what works
steps.narration: Refused fields go grey and only real effort levels are offered.

steps.label: caches result
steps.narration: Saved per endpoint and model, so next time costs zero requests.

deep.algorithm: Learn provider quirks from 400 errors
deep.idea: Send a request, read why the provider refused it, fix the payload, retry, and remember the fix per model.
how: _prepare applies known quirks: reasoning models drop temperature/top_p; OpenAI hosts rename max_tokens.
On a 400, _learn_from_error regex-reads the message: drop or rename the named parameter.
Effort errors move to the nearest level listed in 'Supported values are: …'.
At most 3 adjustments; fixes are cached in _quirks per (base_url, model).
deep.why: There are too many OpenAI-compatible providers to hardcode. Error-driven learning means only the first request per model pays the extra round-trip.
deep.cost: ≤3 extra requests, once per model per process.

stepNotes.3: validate sends {max_tokens:16, temperature:0.5, top_p:0.5, effort}. Example: 400 "Unsupported parameter: 'max_tokens'. Use 'max_completion_tokens' instead" → _learn_from_error renames the parameter and retries. 'Supported values are: low, medium' → nearest effort.
stepNotes.4: Fixes go into _quirks[(normalized base_url, model)] = {param: replacement or None}, so later calls are rewritten before sending. 'use /v1/responses' adds the model to _tools_via_responses, sending tool calls to the Responses API.

nodeNotes.web-app: key-form.tsx debounces 600 ms after a model change, then greys out unsupported fields and lists only real effort levels.
nodeNotes.llm-client: validate, _prepare, _learn_from_error, _learn_effort: a probe-and-adapt loop with per-model memory in process.
nodeNotes.llm-provider: Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint; its 400 error text is the source of truth for what it accepts.
nodeNotes.browser-apis: localStorage 'byos:model-checks' caches {unsupported, efforts} per endpoint and model for 30 days, max 60 entries, no secrets.

features.name: Scoped API keys
features.summary: Keys for your scripts, with exactly the access you give them.
features.description: Give each key its own access level per resource and an expiry, or none at all. The full key shows exactly once, so copy it. You get 10 active keys, and revoking one takes effect immediately.
features.underTheHood: Only a SHA-256 of the key is stored, and a public prefix makes the lookup one query. GET is read, everything else is write. Keys are blocked from account-admin routes, so a leaked key can't mint more keys or read your storage credentials.

steps.label: creates a key
steps.narration: You pick access per resource and an expiry.

steps.label: new key request
steps.narration: Only a logged-in session can make keys. The 10-key limit is checked here.

steps.label: stores the hash
steps.narration: You see the full key once. BYOS keeps only its hash, so don't lose it.

steps.label: Bearer key
steps.narration: Your script calls something like GET /files.

steps.label: checks prefix + scope
steps.narration: The hash is compared, then expiry and scope get checked.

steps.label: per-key rate limit
steps.narration: Each key gets its own counter. If Redis is down, the request goes through anyway.

keyFiles: apps/api/src/byos_api/apikeys/service.py — key format, hashing, scopes, limits
apps/web/lib/limits.ts — client copy of the limits

deep.algorithm: Prefix-indexed, hash-only bearer keys
deep.idea: Keys carry a public prefix for lookup and a secret that is only ever stored as a hash.
how: Key = byosk_<8 hex>_<token_urlsafe(32)>; only sha256(full key) is stored.
authenticate: split, look up by prefix, compare_digest the hash, check expiry and revocation.
require_scope: GET/HEAD/OPTIONS need :read (or :write); others need :write.
Per-key fixed-window limit; SessionUser routes reject keys with 403.
deep.example:
byosk_0a1b2c3d_EXAMPLEnotARealSecret…
POST /files → needs files:write
GET /folders → folders:read or folders:write
deep.why: High-entropy keys don't need slow password hashing; SHA-256 plus an indexed prefix keeps checks fast. Blocking keys from account admin means a leak can't escalate.
deep.cost: One indexed lookup per request.

stepNotes.3: byosk_ + token_hex(4) (8 hex chars, the indexed prefix) + token_urlsafe(32) (the secret). Stored: prefix and sha256(full key). The plaintext appears once in the response and is never logged or stored.
stepNotes.5: Split on '_', SELECT by unique prefix, secrets.compare_digest(sha256(raw), key_hash), then reject if revoked or expired. require_scope: GET/HEAD/OPTIONS → files:read or files:write; POST/PATCH/DELETE → files:write. Sessions skip scopes.
stepNotes.6: INCR rl:apikey:<prefix>; on the first hit EXPIRE 60. Count over 120 → 429. Any Redis exception returns 'allowed': an outage removes throttling but never takes the API down.

nodeNotes.web-app: Per-resource None/Read/Read-and-write pickers map to scopes; the plaintext is shown once with Copy; a meter shows N of 10.
nodeNotes.auth-service: apikeys.service creates, authenticates and revokes keys; dependencies.require_scope maps HTTP methods to read or write.
nodeNotes.postgres: api_keys stores prefix (unique index), key_hash, scopes JSONB, expires_at and last_used_at (touched at most every 5 minutes).
nodeNotes.integrations: The developer's script: sends the key as a Bearer token and must handle 403 (scope) and 429 (rate) responses.
nodeNotes.api-gateway: get_principal detects the byosk_ prefix and builds an api_key Principal; SessionUser routes reject it outright.
nodeNotes.redis: Fixed-window counter rl:apikey:<prefix> with a 60 s expiry. Fails open if Redis is unreachable.

features.name: Signed webhooks
features.summary: Get a signed HTTP call whenever a file changes.
features.description: Add an endpoint URL and choose which file events you care about; none means all of them. Each webhook gets a signing secret, and a sample request shows what will arrive. Up to 5 per account.
features.underTheHood: URLs pointing at private or internal addresses are rejected up front. Deliveries fire in the background, signed with HMAC-SHA256. Redirects are off, so a sneaky URL can't bounce the request somewhere internal. Nothing is retried, so your endpoint had better be awake.

steps.label: adds an endpoint
steps.narration: You paste a URL and pick your events.

steps.label: registers the webhook
steps.narration: The host is looked up and internal IPs get turned away. You get the secret back.

steps.label: file event
steps.narration: An upload commits and the event fires. The upload doesn't wait for it.

steps.label: loads webhooks
steps.narration: It finds the owner's active webhooks, on its own database session.

steps.label: signed POST
steps.narration: Signed, 5 second timeout, no redirects, no second chances.

deep.algorithm: HMAC-signed fire-and-forget POSTs with SSRF guard
deep.idea: Subscribers get a signed JSON POST per file event; the URL is checked against internal networks first.
how: Create: resolve the host via getaddrinfo and reject any private, loopback, link-local, reserved or multicast address.
emit schedules an asyncio task and returns immediately.
_fanout loads active hooks, builds one compact body, and signs it per hook.
POST with X-BYOS-Signature, 5 s timeout, no redirects; failures are dropped.
deep.why: File operations must never wait on a stranger's server. Arq exists as a dependency for retries but isn't wired in. Resolution is checked at creation only, not on each delivery.
deep.cost: No retries; pending deliveries lost on restart.

stepNotes.2: _validate_url: http(s) only (https in production), then getaddrinfo(host). Every resolved IP is checked; is_private, is_loopback, is_link_local, is_reserved, is_multicast or is_unspecified rejects, so http://127.0.0.1 or 10.x can't be targeted.
stepNotes.5: Body {"event":"file.created","data":{"name":"demo.pdf"}} with secret EXAMPLE_SECRET → X-BYOS-Signature: sha256=ed579d89…dfd2c9 (HMAC-SHA256 of the raw bytes). follow_redirects=False, 5 s timeout, no retries; the asyncio task never blocks the upload.

nodeNotes.web-app: Developer settings: URL plus event chips (none means all); shows the masked secret with reveal and copy.
nodeNotes.webhook-dispatcher: service: SSRF check and the 5-hook cap. dispatcher: emit → asyncio task → load hooks → sign → POST, no retries.
nodeNotes.metadata-engine: Calls emit after upload, replace and delete commits, with {file_id, name, size, mime, folder_id}.
nodeNotes.postgres: webhooks rows: url, secret, events JSONB, active; read on a fresh session per delivery.
nodeNotes.integrations: The receiver recomputes HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body with its secret and compares in constant time.

nodes.label: You
nodes.summary: You, running your drive and chatting with Bao.
nodes.details: Owns the storage accounts and the LLM key. Signs in with a Telegram code or a password, then does everything through the web app.

nodes.label: Link Visitor
nodes.summary: Anyone with a link and no account.
nodes.details: Opens permanent links, shared folders or expiring shares without logging in. Files stream straight to the browser; folder links redirect to a page. Every public route is rate-limited per IP.

nodes.label: Web App
nodes.summary: The Next.js app: drive, Bao chat, settings, public pages.
nodes.details: Runs in the browser and talks to the API through a shared SDK. The access token lives only in memory and comes back on reload via an httpOnly cookie. Uploads use XHR for progress.
keyFiles: apps/web/components/byok/drive-chat.tsx — composer, slash commands, stream handling
nodes.interesting: Answers and control events share one plain-text stream, split by an ASCII record separator. No WebSockets, and it all saves as one string.

nodes.label: Your Scripts
nodes.summary: Your own code, calling the API with byosk_ keys.
nodes.details: Sends a Bearer key and gets only what that key's scopes allow, under its own rate limit. Can also receive signed file webhooks, which it should verify before trusting.
keyFiles: docs/DEVELOPERS.md — API reference, scopes, webhook verification

nodes.label: API Gateway
nodes.summary: The FastAPI front door: auth checks, rate limits, error mapping.
nodes.details: Every request passes through here. It mounts the routers, registers the public link catch-all last, and turns storage failures into errors naming the broken provider. A daily task deletes week-old AI chats.
keyFiles: apps/api/src/byos_api/main.py — app factory, error handlers, the daily cleanup task
apps/api/src/byos_api/core/ratelimit.py — fixed-window limiter that fails open
nodes.interesting: Even 500 errors get CORS headers, because the error-catching middleware sits inside CORS. A small mercy for whoever is debugging.

nodes.label: Auth & Keys
nodes.summary: Logins, sessions, API keys and the audit log.
nodes.details: Turns each request into a session with full access or an API key with limited scopes. Access tokens last 15 minutes. Refresh tokens last 30 days, rotate on every use and are stored hashed.
keyFiles: apps/api/src/byos_api/audit/recorder.py — audit writer that never raises
nodes.interesting: Audit logs store IPs only as salted hashes, so even the logs can't say where you were.

nodes.label: Metadata Engine
nodes.summary: Everything about your files except the actual bytes.
nodes.details: Runs the virtual file system: folders, versions, tags, search and duplicate checks. It picks where uploads go, hands bytes to the storage adapters and fires file events. Bao's write tools call the same functions.
nodes.interesting: The duplicate check runs after the upload, because the hash isn't known until then. A retried upload gets stored, spotted, then deleted.

nodes.label: Links Service
nodes.summary: Creates and serves permanent links, shared folders and expiring shares.
nodes.details: Owners create links; anyone can open them, 120 requests a minute per IP. File links stream the current version. Expired shares return 410. If the owner's GitHub or S3 keys broke, visitors get a plain 503; a dead Telegram session comes back as a 409.
keyFiles: apps/api/src/byos_api/aliases/router.py — owner CRUD, public resolver, /public folder API
nodes.interesting: The ETag is the content hash. Unchanged file? A 304, and Telegram never even hears about it.

nodes.label: Storage Adapters
nodes.summary: One storage interface, with Telegram, GitHub and S3 behind it.
nodes.details: Each adapter translates its backend's errors into plain ones, including 'these credentials are dead'. Credentials are stored encrypted. Disconnecting GitHub or S3 wipes the credentials but keeps the row while files still point at it. Disconnecting Telegram logs out and deletes it.
nodes.interesting: There's no replace method. Telegram messages and release assets are basically append-only, so every backend uploads new and moves a pointer.

nodes.label: Webhooks
nodes.summary: Stores webhook subscriptions and sends signed file events.
nodes.details: Checks URLs, caps you at 5, then delivers in a background task with a signature and a 5 second timeout. Failed deliveries are logged and dropped. A restart loses anything still pending.
keyFiles: apps/api/src/byos_api/webhooks/service.py — subscription CRUD and SSRF guard
nodes.interesting: Redirects are off on purpose. Otherwise a URL that passed the private-IP check could redirect itself somewhere internal.

nodes.label: Bao Agent
nodes.summary: The loop that answers questions and drafts plans you review.
nodes.details: Each turn is up to 10 model steps, or 30 when organising. Read tools run right away. Writes run or wait, depending on your mode. It also applies and revises plans, and re-runs failed actions.
nodes.interesting: Plans live on the server, not in the browser, so Apply can only run what the model actually proposed.

nodes.label: Index & Retrieval
nodes.summary: Chunks your files, then finds the right ones with pgvector.
nodes.details: Indexing extracts text, sends near-blank pages to your vision model, cuts text into 1,800-character chunks and stores their embeddings. Search asks Postgres to rank them with pgvector, then the add-ons tidy things up and hits get spread across files. It also checks citations.
keyFiles: apps/api/src/byos_api/ai/semantic.py — embedding cache and cosine ranking
nodes.interesting: Search happens inside Postgres: pgvector sorts chunks by cosine distance and only the top few rows ever leave. The column stays a plain float array, so any embedding size fits.

nodes.label: LLM Client
nodes.summary: One client for any OpenAI-compatible provider, on your key.
nodes.details: Handles chat, tool calls, vision and embeddings against any base URL. If a provider rejects a parameter, it adjusts the request and remembers the fix. Bad keys and rate limits get separate errors.
keyFiles: apps/api/tests/test_llm_params.py — tests for adapting rejected parameters
nodes.interesting: Reasoning-effort levels are rarely documented, so the client reads 'Supported values are: ...' from the error message and picks the closest.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.summary: The source of truth. Everything except the bytes lives here.
nodes.details: 19 tables across 26 migrations, covering users, files, versions, links, keys, embeddings and Bao's plans. It's also the search engine: pgvector ranks chunk embeddings, and a full-text column plus a trigram index handle file names. Production runs on Supabase in Mumbai.
nodes.interesting: The API-to-database round trip is the main cost per request, so hosting was weighed by how close it sits to this. The free plan settles for Singapore, about 50 ms from Mumbai.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.summary: Optional rate limits and a tiny cache. Nobody misses it.
nodes.details: Counts requests for rate limits and caches the storage overview for 30 seconds. Runs locally in docker-compose, but production skips it for now, so rate limits are effectively off there.
nodes.interesting: Everything fails open. If Redis dies, you lose rate limits and caching, and the API carries on.

nodes.label: Telegram
nodes.summary: Your Telegram account. It's your login and your default storage.
nodes.details: Files are sent as documents to your Saved Messages and fetched by message id on every download. BYOS caps files at 2 GB; Premium's 4 GB needs the server limit raised. Flood limits become 'try again in N s'.
nodes.interesting: End your Telegram sessions and BYOS notices, then politely asks you to sign in again.

nodes.label: GitHub Releases
nodes.summary: Files stored as release assets in your own repo.
nodes.details: BYOS makes the repo, private by default, with one commit so releases can be tagged. Uploads land on a daily prerelease. Downloads follow GitHub's redirect to a signed URL.
nodes.interesting: GitHub sends the token's expiry date on every response, so BYOS can warn you before it runs out.

nodes.label: S3 Bucket
nodes.summary: Any S3-compatible bucket you connect.
nodes.details: Each file is stored under its own uuid path. boto3 runs in worker threads and makes up to 3 attempts per call. Dead keys and keys missing a permission get different error messages.

nodes.label: Your LLM
nodes.summary: Your LLM endpoint and models, on your saved key.
nodes.details: Does chat, tool calls, embeddings, vision and the model list. Your key is stored encrypted and only decrypted to make these calls, or when you hit Reveal (which gets logged).

nodes.label: Keep-warm Cron
nodes.summary: Pokes the app every 5 minutes so it doesn't nap.
nodes.details: A Google Apps Script hits the web app and the API's /ping, because Render's free tier falls asleep after about 15 idle minutes.
nodes.interesting: Keeping both awake all month needs about 1,490 instance-hours. The free tier gives 750. The script's own notes admit this.

nodes.label: Browser APIs
nodes.summary: Device stuff: storage, sound, vibration, PDF rendering, clipboard.
nodes.details: Holds per-device preferences, recents, your selected key and mode, and cached model checks. Almost every storage read and write is wrapped, so private windows mostly still work. PDFs for highlighting render with pdf.js.
nodes.interesting: No sound files ship with the app. Every click and chime is generated live with Web Audio, a few milliseconds at a time.
